Article Title: Ariane Gorin CEO of Expedia, world’s second-largest online travel company, says: Everyone knows role of CEO is to set strategy, but biggest thing I have learnt is that it is also setting right ...
Article Text:
Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says AI is changing the travel industry



Expedia's approach to AI and travel

Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says leading a company in the AI era is about more than defining business strategy and building leadership teams. Speaking about her experience since taking over as chief executive in 2024, Gorin said one of the biggest lessons she has learned is that a CEO is also responsible for shaping an organisation's culture.In an interview with The Financial Times, Gorin said, “Everyone knows the role of the CEO is to set the strategy and build the right team. But I think the biggest thing I’ve learnt is that the role of the CEO is also setting the culture.” Her comments come as investors, employees and travel industry partners increasingly focus on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the online travel business.Expedia, the world's second-largest online travel company after Booking Holdings, acknowledged in its annual report earlier this year that advances in generative AI and autonomous AI agents capable of planning and booking trips could change the competitive landscape. However, Gorin said she sees AI as an opportunity to improve operations and help travellers make better decisions.According to Gorin, companies across the travel sector are actively discussing how AI can be deployed, with many sharing ideas despite competing with one another.“Everyone in the industry is figuring out how we can use AI . . . and I feel like it’s similar to what happened in Covid, where you had companies that were competing against each other actually come together and say, ‘You know what: how do we work together to convince governments to open borders?’”She added, “There’s something similar right now in the industry as I talk to colleagues and peers where people [are] really trying to say, ‘What are you finding? How are you using it? What are the real opportunities?’ Because there’s so much hype out there.”Gorin said AI has also changed the way she works. She explained that meeting notes, including partner backgrounds and suggested business opportunities, are increasingly prepared using AI, reducing tasks that previously took significant time.She also said she sets aside two hours every Sunday to experiment with AI tools and competing products to better understand developments in the industry.Despite acknowledging AI's growing role, Gorin said she does not believe it will replace every aspect of travel planning.“Some people will want to be end-to-end agentic and we will be there for them [but] a lot of people actually enjoy the process of planning a trip. In fact, people are happiest when they’re planning the trip — they’re even happier than when they’re on it,” she noted.Gorin also said travel bookings differ from many other online purchases because they involve changes, cancellations and customer support after a booking is made.“Travel is not like buying a T-shirt,” she noted.She added that Expedia continues to focus on loyalty benefits and customer support as it adapts to AI-driven changes in the travel industry.Gorin became Expedia's chief executive in May 2024 after previously leading the company's business-to-business division. Under her leadership, Expedia has continued expanding its AI capabilities while managing brands including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.
Article Summary: Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin says a CEO is also responsible for shaping an organisation's culture. Gorin's comments come as investors, employees and travel industry partners increasingly focus on how artificial intelligence is reshaping the online travel business. Expedia acknowledged in its annual report that advances in generative AI and autonomous AI agents could change the competitive landscape.

Article Title: Google founder Sergey Brin’s Coalition gets into action, reserves nearly $87 million of advertising time across California State to show TV ads on ...
Article Text:
Sergey Brin

Billionaires’ ‘counter measure’ strategy

A coalition of billionaires led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly planning a massive campaign to defeat a proposed state wealth tax. The coalition has reserved nearly $87 million in television advertising time across California, as per a report by The New York Times. This signals the start of a ‘battle’ over a November ballot initiative that would slap a one-time tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion or more.The ad campaign is set to kick off next month, and reportedly represents the opening salvo in a political war that has deeply divided Silicon Valley, state lawmakers and labor unions. Citing tracking data from AdImpact, the coalition – operating under the name Building A Better California – has already locked in $86.9 million for TV ads. The campaign will scale up, with over $53 million allocated for September alone.Industry experts expect the total cost of the campaign to climb significantly higher, as the current buy includes only $3.7 million reserved for October, traditionally the heaviest month for political advertising in California, the report said.Citing state campaign finance records, the report says that Brin has personally funneled roughly $82 million, emerging as the primary leader of the pushback.Brin has recruited other prominent Silicon Valley figures to join the cause, including venture capital titans John Doerr and Michael Moritz.Rather than simply campaigning against the wealth tax, Brin’s coalition has executed a classic California political maneuver: placing two competing tax measures on the same ballot to invalidate or confuse the original proposal. Under California law, if both the billionaire tax and a conflicting counter-measure pass in November, the initiative that receives the highest total number of “yes” votes takes effect.“Our coalition is committed to ensuring that all California voters are informed about policies that impact our state’s future and economy. The measures we support provide important and common-sense protections designed to improve state accountability and governance and protect California families from new taxes on their retirement and savings,” said coalition spokeswoman Abby Lunardini.The proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, is backed by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), which spent $31 million to place the measure on the ballot. The measure has drawn support from progressive leaders, including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.
Article Summary: A coalition of billionaires led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly planning a massive campaign to defeat a proposed state wealth tax. The coalition has reserved nearly $87 million in television advertising time across California, as per a report by The New York Times. This signals the start of a ‘battle’ over a November ballot initiative that would slap a one-time tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion or more.

Dell expects annual AI server sales to exceed $60 billion. Michael Dell's fortune has also grown sharply over the past few years, rising from $22.9 billion in 2020 to more than $221 billion today, according to Forbes.Meta is scheduled to report its quarterly results next week, while Dell Technologies is expected to announce its second-quarter earnings next month.

Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O'Leary on AI data center causing water scarcity; says: Those days are gone, now it is like ...
Article Text:
Kevin O'Leary says newer data centers use less water



Kevin O’Leary calls for AI data centers to generate their own power



Kevin O'Leary is not convinced that modern AI data centers are driving water scarcity in the way critics often claim. Speaking during a recent appearance on Glenn Beck's radio show, the Canadian billionaire and "Shark Tank" investor argued that advances in cooling technology have significantly reduced water consumption, saying "those days are gone" and comparing today's facilities to "a golf course" in terms of water use.Referring to his company’s planned data center project in Utah, O'Leary said the first phase of the development, with 1.4 gigawatts of power capacity, would be "no different than a golf course" when it comes to water consumption. "Because data centers, not just my project," O'Leary said, "any new data center now is like a golf course."O'Leary, whose company O'Leary Ventures is developing AI data centers in Utah and Canada, said concerns over water usage are based on older facilities rather than modern infrastructure.Speaking on the radio show, O'Leary said, “The new modern era data center does not require anywhere near the water that was used 15 years ago in Virginia, where data centers got a bad name because of how much water they consume.”Data centers use water directly for cooling servers and indirectly through the electricity required to power them. However, some technology companies have argued that newer cooling systems, including closed-loop technologies, have reduced water consumption compared with older facilities.Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also rejected claims that AI services consume large amounts of water."Water is totally fake," Altman said, when asked about concerns over AI companies' water use. "It used to be true, we used to do evaporative cooling in data centers, but now that we don't do that, you know, you see these like things on the internet where, 'Don't use ChatGPT, it's 17 gallons of water for each query' or whatever,” he added.A previous Business Insider investigation found that some of the largest data center facilities in the US were permitted to use more water each day than nearly 49,000 Americans would typically consume.O'Leary also argued that future data center projects should be responsible for building their own electricity infrastructure rather than relying entirely on existing power grids."The new rule of engagement should be this — as part of the national solution is — if I'm going to bring a data center anywhere, I've got to bring my own power. I got to spend billions to build power, and then give some of it back to the grid, so we can stay competitive,” he said.Meanwhile, O'Leary is facing a defamation lawsuit over comments he made during multiple media appearances in which he accused some opponents of his Utah data center project of being backed by the Chinese Communist Party. Before the lawsuit was filed, O'Leary said on social media that he had no evidence that the project's critics were funded by China.Jeffrey Neiman, an attorney representing O'Leary, previously told Business Insider in a statement that his client intends to "defend this lawsuit vigorously" and file counterclaims. Neiman also described the lawsuit as a "cash grab."
Article Summary: Kevin O'Leary says AI data centers use less water than in the past. The Canadian billionaire said advances in cooling technology have significantly reduced water consumption. He also argued that future data center projects should be responsible for building their own electricity infrastructure rather than relying on existing power grids.

Article Title: Pentagon is angry with Dean W Ball, top executive of Sam Altman's OpenAI, calls him 'supreme village idiot' and reminds him that US government passed a law in 2026 that restricts ...
Article Text:
What caused the feud

Pentagon fires back: ‘Not some deep state scheme’

A feud has erupted between senior Trump administration officials and a top executive at Sam Altman’s OpenAI . In a series of public attacks, Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael slammed OpenAI’s Head of Strategic Futures Dean W. Ball, calling him the industry’s “supreme village idiot”. The exchange was triggered by comments Ball made regarding how the US government should handle the rising threat of open-source Chinese AI models, following the launch of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.The controversy began over the weekend when Ball, a former White House architect of the administration's AI Action Plan who recently joined OpenAI, posted his thoughts on how to stop American companies from adopting Chinese AI systems.Ball suggested that rather than outright banning open-source software, the Trump administration should intentionally spread "FUD" (Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt) by issuing regulatory warnings to scare private companies away from using Chinese models like DeepSeek.“I would guess that the Trump Administration will at some point realize that their best strategy here would be to create large amounts of regulatory risk around the use of open-weight Chinese models.You don't need to "ban open source" (one of the dumber motifs of AI policy discussion). You just need to direct every agency to issue soft law that creates FUD,” he said.“‘A Federal Reserve Advisory Bulletin found that there may be backdoors in Chinese AI models.’ It needn't be that well justified. You just create enough regulatory risk that every regulated enterprise backs off. You probably don't want to create so much regulatory risk that you scare off the hyperscalers from serving Chinese models; this will just drive startups to sketchier providers. There's a happy middle ground here. I'd assume they will do some version of this,” he addedThe comments immediately drew fire from White House AI adviser David Sacks, who questioned whether Ball was advocating for “regulatory capture”, a tactic that would directly benefit his new employer, OpenAI, by driving enterprise customers away from free Chinese alternatives towards the proprietary American providers.“The departments of war, transportation, energy, agriculture, commerce, NASA, and Congress have all blocked their employees from using Chinese AI, citing ill-justified claims of danger. This already has sent a message to regulated firms. All of this happened during this admin,” he said.When Ball defended his position by pointing out that federal agencies like the Department of Defense (DoD) have already banned employees from using Chinese AI tools, the Pentagon responded with anger. Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael unleashed a series of personal attacks, reminding Ball that restrictions on Chinese software were legally enacted by lawmakers, not cooked up behind closed doors.“Every industry/ecosystem has its supreme village idiot. @deanwball is that for AI. Congress passed a law in 2026 that restricted some uses of DeepSeek/High Flyer with waivers permitted. Only those models. It went through the democratic process not some Deep State scheme like he would prefer. Dean Ball has perhaps the biggest gap between actual IQ and his own perceived IQ of anyone in the industry (about 40 points),” Michael wrote on X.Michael emphasised that the Pentagon's restrictions were designed strictly to keep military IT systems from connecting to foreign adversary networks.“So let me get this straight @deanwball. This was about ensuring that DoD IT networks were not connected to adversary networks. You think your deep state regulatory capture scheme is equivalent to making sure our warfighter networks are not compromised? I take it back: 50 IQ difference (75 versus 125). Take a breather and enjoy the match,” he added.
Article Summary: Pentagon fires back: ‘Not some deep state scheme’ A feud has erupted between senior Trump administration officials and a top executive at OpenAI. Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael slammed OpenAI’s Head of Strategic Futures Dean W. Ball. The exchange was triggered by comments Ball made regarding how the US government should handle the rising threat of open-source Chinese AI.

Article Title: Engineers building Solar panels are using exact replicas of honeycombs made by Bees to ensure ...
Article Text:
How bee honeycombs could make solar panels more efficient



Tests show big gains in power outpuT

Bees may have helped solve one of solar energy's biggest problems. According to a report by Ecoportal, engineers have developed a new type of solar panel using the honeycomb pattern that bees have mastered for millions of years. The idea is simple. Traditional solar panels lose a lot of sunlight when the sun is not directly overhead because the light bounces off the surface. The new honeycomb-inspired design traps more of that light instead of reflecting it. Early tests suggest the approach could significantly improve power generation while making solar panels more useful on a wider range of surfaces.One of the biggest challenges with today's solar panels is that they work best only when sunlight falls directly on them. As the sun moves during the day, the light hits the panels at an angle. A large part of that light gets reflected instead of being turned into electricity.To fix this, engineers looked to nature for inspiration. They created a 3D concave solar panel based on the same hexagonal honeycomb structure built by bees. Instead of allowing sunlight to bounce away, the angled walls inside the structure make the light bounce from one surface to another.This gives the panel another chance to absorb the energy.According to the researchers quoted in the report, the new design increased maximum power output by 142.3% compared with a conventional flat solar panel under the same conditions. Even when sunlight hit the panel straight on, power output improved by 36.4%. At a 60-degree angle, where traditional panels usually struggle the most, performance increased by 61.8%.The team also used a flexible 3D polymer metamaterial to support the honeycomb structure. This means the design could eventually be used on curved buildings, electric vehicles and even aerospace equipment, instead of being limited to flat rooftops.
Article Summary: Engineers have developed a new type of solar panel using the honeycomb pattern that bees have mastered for millions of years. Traditional solar panels lose a lot of sunlight when the sun is not directly overhead because the light bounces off the surface. The new honeycomb-inspired design traps more of that light instead of reflecting it.

Article Title: Auto industry analysts are worried about Tesla and other car makers using the technology that Google, Apple, Samsung and other smartphone companies have been using since over ten years to update their
Article Text:
OTA updates raise cybersecurity concerns: Analyst



Norwegian bus test highlights potential risks



Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates, a technology that smartphone companies like Google, Apple and Samsung have relied on for more than a decade to deliver new features and security fixes. While the technology has made updating vehicles faster and cheaper, cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks. According to a CNBC report, analysts say wireless updates could leave connected vehicles vulnerable to cyberattacks, data breaches and even attempts by foreign actors to interfere with vehicle systems.Over-the-air (OTA) technology allows manufacturers to wirelessly send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center.Tesla began rolling out OTA updates for its Model S vehicles in 2012, helping popularize the technology across the automotive industry. Today, many car makers use OTA updates to improve vehicle software and fix issues remotely."The technology is increasingly welcomed as it is a quick and cost-effective way to manage systems on vehicles, over traditional methods which may have required a recall or update at routine maintenance," Siraj Ahmed Shaikh, professor in systems security at Swansea University in the UK, told CNBC.However, analysts say the growing use of OTA updates also introduces new cybersecurity risks.Its use represents "a unique national security concern," Gabriel Lim, senior analyst at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told CNBC."Aside from data privacy concerns, the potential of a foreign actor sabotaging the controls of a moving vehicle is a possibility that countries like Norway, Denmark, and Britain have expressed concerns about," Lim added.The concerns gained attention after Norwegian public transport company Ruter tested two buses last year and found potential security risks linked to OTA technology."There is access to the control system for battery and power supply via mobile network through a Romanian SIM card. In theory, therefore, this bus can be stopped or rendered inoperable by the manufacturer," the company said.The findings prompted authorities in the UK and Denmark to launch their own investigations.
Article Summary: Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates. The technology allows manufacturers to send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center. But cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks.

Article Text:

Why the EU has fined AliExpress

Alibaba's AliExpress is facing a record fine in Europe. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the European Commission has imposed a €550 million ($630 million) penalty after concluding that the e-commerce platform failed to adequately address the sale of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products, in breach of the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA).Explaining the decision, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said the issue posed risks beyond regulatory compliance.she told reporters. Virkkunen noted that AliExpress had 193 million users in Europe last year, compared with 156 million for Shein and 130 million for Temu, adding that one in five Europeans shop on the three platforms at least once a month.The €550 million penalty is the third issued by the European Commission under the DSA, which requires very large online platforms to assess and mitigate risks posed by illegal and harmful content. Reuters reported that the fine is higher than the €200 million penalty imposed on Temu in May and the €120 million fine issued to Elon Musk's social media platform, X, in December last year, for DSA violations.According to the European Commission, AliExpress did not properly assess whether it had sufficient staff to review risks associated with illegal products and overestimated the effectiveness of its systems for detecting and removing such listings.The regulator also said the platform's recommender and advertising systems contributed to the spread of illegal products. It criticised AliExpress for relying on a single quantitative indicator to assess the effectiveness of its moderation system and said illegal listings, including counterfeit products, unsafe toys and dangerous cosmetics, remained available for weeks.The Commission further said the company's penalty system was ineffective because sellers that had been penalised were still able to continue offering illegal products. It also found that AliExpress' mandatorysystem, intended to prevent counterfeit sales, was understaffed and could be easily bypassed by traders selling fake goods.AliExpress said it will appeal the fine, describing it as excessive. The company told Reuters,The company also said it has worked with the European Commission to meet itsThe report added that the Commission first charged AliExpress in June last year with failing to comply with DSA requirements to assess and mitigate the risks of illegal products. The company has until October 20 to propose additional remedial measures and could face further penalties if regulators decide in December that those measures do not comply with the law.The Commission said the novelty of the DSA was considered a mitigating factor while calculating the penalty, adding that the fine could otherwise have been higher. AliExpress had previously avoided a separate fine in June last year after agreeing to measures aimed at limiting the spread of potentially illegal and pornographic material on its platform.
Article Summary: Alibaba's AliExpress is facing a record fine in Europe. The European Commission has imposed a €550 million ($630 million) penalty. The e-commerce platform failed to adequately address the sale of illegal, unsafe and counterfeit products, in breach of the European Union's Digital Services Act.

Article Title: Trump's AI security agency head resigns after 3 months; Arvind Raman named acting chief
Article Text:
NIST academic to take over



Chris Fall, the head of the United States Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), has resigned just three months after taking charge of the federal artificial intelligence (AI) testing institute. According to Axios, the US Commerce Department confirmed the departure, announcing that Dr. Arvind Raman, Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), will step in to serve as the acting director of the agency.The resignation comes at a crucial moment as the Trump administration grapples with setting safety guidelines, evaluation benchmarks and national standards for rapidly evolving AI technologies. Fall was appointed in April to lead the newly-reorganised federal body.CAISI was established after the administration restructured the former US AI Safety Institute, and it is tasked with developing rigorous testing capabilities and evaluation protocols to ensure advanced AI systems can be deployed safely without posing national security risks.A Commerce Department official clarified that his tenure was always intended to be temporary to help set up the agency's foundational framework.“Following Chris's departure, NIST Director Dr. Arvind Raman will continue to oversee CAISI and will serve as Acting CAISI Director,” Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said in an official statement to the publication.Dr. Arvind Raman, an academic and former dean of engineering at Purdue University, who was officially sworn in as the director of NIST on June 30, will now dual-hat his duties. He will lead both NIST and CAISI while the administration searches for a permanent replacement. According to department officials, Raman has spent several weeks interviewing potential candidates to take over CAISI permanently.However, until a permanent appointment is finalised, the federal AI safety office will operate under temporary leadership during a delicate period.
Article Summary: Chris Fall, the head of the United States Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), has resigned. Fall was appointed in April to lead the newly-reorganised federal body. Dr. Arvind Raman, Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), will step in to serve as the acting director of the agency.

Article Title: Salesforce launches SMB growth kit for small businesses in India
Article Text: Salesforce has announced the SMB Growth Kit, a connected platform designed specifically for India’s small and medium businesses. The offering brings Agentforce Sales, Slack and Tableau together, helping SMBs replace disconnected tools with a unified system that improves visibility, accelerates collaboration and supports revenue growth. Salesforce says businesses can go live in four to six weeks.Agentforce Sales gives SMBs a real-time view of every lead, opportunity and pipeline, eliminating reliance on spreadsheets or manual updates. Automated lead assignment, workflow automation and mobile access help sales teams move faster. Built‑in AI capabilities — including opportunity scoring, forecasting and intelligent recommendations — allow teams to focus on high‑value opportunities without specialist expertise.Slack serves as the collaboration layer for SMBs adopting new technology. Already familiar to many growing businesses, Slack enables teams across sales, support, HR, IT and operations to work together in one place. For smaller teams where employees juggle multiple responsibilities, Slack helps save time and keep work moving efficiently.Tableau turns business data into actionable insights through live, mobile‑friendly dashboards.Founders and business leaders can monitor pipeline health, revenue trends and overall performance without waiting for static reports. Its drag‑and‑drop interface makes analytics accessible to all users, while native Salesforce connectivity provides real‑time visibility without complex integrations.Together, Agentforce Sales, Slack and Tableau form a single operating system that helps Indian SMBs sell smarter, collaborate faster and make confident decisions. The SMB Growth Kit includes structured onboarding, hands‑on setup and post‑go‑live support, enabling teams to adopt AI‑ready systems without operational burden. The offering will be delivered through select Salesforce reseller partners across India.Mankiran Chowhan, Managing Director, Salesforce India, said the challenge for SMBs is scattered customer data, conversations and insights. “SMB Growth Kit gives growing businesses one connected system where sales activity, team conversations and live insights work together — helping teams act with more confidence, fewer blind spots and less guesswork.”The SMB Growth Kit is available immediately for small and medium businesses in India through select Salesforce reseller partners. Salesforce teams will support customers with onboarding, setup and post‑go‑live assistance, with businesses expected to be live within four to six weeks.
Article Summary: Salesforce has announced the SMB Growth Kit, a connected platform designed specifically for India's small and medium businesses. Quote of the day by Nikola Tesla

"If you want to find the secrets of the universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration."

The meaning behind the quote

Why is the quote associated with Nikola Tesla

Why the quote continues to be shared

Nikola Tesla is often credited with one of the most widely shared quotes about understanding the universe through science:The statement continues to be referenced in discussions around physics, innovation and Tesla's approach to understanding the natural world.The quote reflects Tesla's belief that many natural phenomena can be understood by studying how energy behaves and how frequency and vibration influence physical systems. While the wording is frequently attributed to Tesla, it has been widely circulated over the years in books, speeches and online discussions.The quote suggests approaching the universe through measurable physical principles rather than appearances alone. In physics, energy is the ability to do work. Frequency is the number of times that something that repeats happens in a given amount of time. Vibration is an oscillating motion.Together, these concepts help explain phenomena ranging from sound and light to electricity and electromagnetic waves. The quote has therefore been interpreted as an encouragement to examine the fundamental forces that shape the physical world.Tesla was an inventor and electrical engineer whose work on alternating current (AC) power systems, electric motors, wireless transmission and high-frequency electrical experiments influenced the development of modern electrical engineering.Much of his research focused on electricity, magnetism and resonant systems, making the themes of energy, frequency and vibration closely associated with his scientific work.The statement is often quoted in discussions of science, engineering and innovation because it links complex physical ideas with a simple way of thinking about the natural world. Article Title: Sergey Brin’s invention saved my eyes, says analyst Patrick Hedger as Senator Bernie Sanders slams him for spending $82 million to 'fight' California’s Wealth Tax on billionaires

How the California billionaire tax would work—and who pays

The measure would require the state to spend 90% of the revenue on healthcare, pitched as an offset to health cuts in President Trump's spending law. California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office found the tax would likely raise tens of billions upfront, but warned some billionaires would leave, shrinking future income tax revenue by hundreds of millions a year. Governor Gavin Newsom, eyeing a 2028 presidential run, opposes it, arguing wealth is mobile and shops for low-tax states.Brin is not alone. John Doerr has given $10 million, with Michael Moritz, Patrick Collison, and Eric Schmidt among the tech names funding the pushback—over $120 million combined against roughly $31 million backing the tax. Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott: "How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy. Intention and…" - a powerful lesson on generosity, giving and why phi
Article Text:
Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott

Quote of the day by MacKenzie Scott

"How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy. Intention and effort makes it philanthropy"

Where this line actually comes from

What the quote is actually arguing

Why intention needs effort attached to it

Why this reframing matters

Other famous quotes by MacKenzie Scott

"People who have experience with inequities are the ones best equipped to design solutions."

"There's no wrong way to give away a fortune."

"The immediate and knock-on benefits of humanitarian speech and compassionate action rarely get mentioned."

Why this quote is relevant today

Philanthropy usually gets measured in figures large enough to make headlines. MacKenzie Scott, who has given away billions of dollars since 2020, argued the actual number was never the point. "How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy," she wrote. "Intention and effort make it philanthropy. If we acknowledge what it all has in common, there will be more of it." She made this argument in a post where she deliberately withheld how much she had actually given away, choosing to reframe the entire conversation rather than let the total dollar figure dominate the story the way it usually does with her announcements, and rather than let her own gift overshadow the far smaller, quieter acts of generosity she was actually trying to defend.Scott wrote this in a Medium post titled "No Dollar Signs This Time," published in December 2021, and deliberately left out the total amount she had donated in that specific round of giving. The omission was intentional. She wanted attention to move away from the dollar figure entirely and toward the underlying idea that generosity takes many forms beyond writing a large cheque.In that same post, she named real, ordinary examples to make the point concrete: donating old furniture to a local shelter, speaking up for a bullied classmate, shovelling a sick neighbour's driveway, staying after a school dance to help stack chairs.None of these involve a financial transaction of any real size. All of them, in her framing, still count as philanthropy.A large donation naturally attracts attention, but the size alone says nothing about the intention or effort behind it. A modest contribution from someone with very little to spare can involve genuine sacrifice, while a much larger sum from someone extremely wealthy might barely register as a cost at all. Scott's point is that philanthropy should be judged by what actually motivated it and what work went into it, not simply by comparing numbers.Caring about a cause is not the same as doing something about it. Scott pairs intention with effort deliberately, since good intentions that never turn into action do not actually help anyone. That effort can be financial, but it can just as easily be time, skill, or sustained attention to a problem that others have simply looked past.Tyrone Freeman, a professor at Indiana University's Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, responded publicly to Scott's post, arguing that an excessive focus on the size of financial gifts, reinforced by tax policy, has narrowed how people imagine giving, who counts as a giver, and how often ordinary generosity actually happens. Scott's post was, in effect, a direct challenge to that narrow definition.Philanthropy tends to be discussed almost entirely through large, newsworthy figures, major grants, billion-dollar pledges, headline donations. Scott's quote pushes back against that framing directly, arguing that the person who quietly helps a struggling neighbour is participating in exactly the same thing as the billionaire announcing a nine-figure gift, provided the intention and the effort behind it are genuinely there.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott has given away billions of dollars since 2020. Scott: "How much or how little money changes hands doesn't make it philanthropy" Philanthropy should be judged by what actually motivated it and what work went into it.

A malicious dataset injected into the system exploited two separate code-execution flaws. Once inside, the autonomous AI agent escalated its access to gain control over internal server nodes, harvested security credentials and moved laterally across several internal server clusters over a weekend.Notably, it was the scale and speed of the hacking incident that caught the attention. According to Huggin Face, the hacker deployed an autonomous agent framework that executed thousands of coordinated actions across a fleet of temporary sandboxes.Secondly, the AI system dynamically shifted its command-and-control operations across public cloud services to evade traditional security filters. Hugging Face confirmed that while unauthorised access to a limited set of internal datasets and service credentials occurred, there is no evidence that public user-facing models, datasets or software packages were tampered with.“The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker,” the company said.When Hugging Face engineers rushed to analyse server logs, they hit a roadblock. The team initially tried using commercial, top-tier AI models via cloud APIs to analyse the malicious code. However, the safety guardrails built into these commercial AI services flagged the actual attack payloads as harmful content, instantly locking out the cybersecurity responders.To bypass the lockout, Hugging Face ran GLM 5.2 – an open-weight AI model by Chinese technology company Z.ai – locally on its own private infrastructure. This allowed defenders to analyse the malicious attack data freely while ensuring sensitive internal tokens never left their secure environment.“The attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried,” Hugging Face noted, pointing out a critical gap in corporate cybersecurity.

Article Title: Kimi K3 AI Model : After 'erasing' America's AI lead, China's Kimi K3 AI model discovers its problems are no different from American AI models ChatGPT and Claude; says: We are temporarily pausing...
Article Text:
Kimi K3 beat Claude in coding tests and spooked Wall Street—then ran out of GPUs, just like ChatGPT and Claude before it.

Kimi K3's viral demand outran Moonshot AI's GPU capacity in 48 hours

Why Moonshot is splitting Kimi memberships into web and coding plans

Kimi K3 open-weight release on July 27 could ease the subscription crunch

China's Moonshot AI spent the past week being the most talked-about name in artificial intelligence. Its new open model, Kimi K3, beat Anthropic's Fable 5 in front-end coding tests, rattled the Nasdaq, and had Silicon Valley executives arguing about whether China had just erased America's lead overnight. For a Beijing startup backed by Alibaba and Tencent, it was the kind of moment most AI labs spend years chasing.Then reality arrived in the form of a bill nobody could pay fast enough—compute. In a post on X, the company admitted its servers simply couldn't keep up. "Kimi K3 has received far more love than we expected, and our GPUs are feeling it," Moonshot wrote, announcing it was hitting pause on new sign-ups. The irony wasn't lost on anyone: the model built to challenge ChatGPT and Claude had just run headfirst into the exact same problem those American models have been wrestling with for years.The numbers moved quickly. Within 48 hours of launch, demand pushed Moonshot's infrastructure "close to the limits of our current capacity," the company said. Its fix was blunt—freeze new subscriptions, protect existing subscribers, and buy time. Current paying users won't be affected, and Moonshot promised to reopen spots "in batches" as it adds capacity.This is familiar territory. OpenAI paused ChatGPT Plus sign-ups in late 2023 when a product launch overwhelmed its systems.Anthropic has rolled out usage caps on Claude for the same reason. Serving a frontier model at scale is expensive and hardware-constrained, and Kimi K3 is heavier than most—a 2.8-trillion-parameter system that Moonshot recommends running on setups with 64 or more accelerators. Popularity, for an AI company, is a cost centre before it's a revenue line.Moonshot is also using the crunch to restructure how it sells access. Going forward, membership splits into two tracks—Kimi Membership covering the web app, mobile app and Kimi Work, and a separate Kimi Code Membership aimed at coding workflows. The logic is operational rather than cosmetic. Coding sessions are compute-hungry and run long, so separating them lets Moonshot match GPUs to demand instead of spreading capacity thin across every use case.The bottleneck may be short-lived. Moonshot plans to release Kimi K3's full model weights by July 27, letting companies and governments download, customise and run the model on their own hardware. That open-weight approach is the whole pitch—and it doubles as a pressure valve, since heavy users can self-host instead of leaning on Moonshot's strained API.For now, though, the takeaway is grounded. Kimi K3 proved a Chinese lab can build near-frontier AI at roughly 40% less cost than its US rivals. What this week also proved is that closing the capability gap doesn't close the compute gap. Whether you're in Beijing or San Francisco, the GPUs run out the same way—and the bill comes due just as fast.
Article Summary: Kimi K3's viral demand outran Moonshot AI's GPU capacity in 48 hours. Within 48 hours of launch, demand pushed Moonshot's infrastructure "close to the limits of our current capacity" Kimi K3 proved a Chinese lab can build near-frontier AI at roughly 40% less cost than its US rivals.

Article Title: Why Jony Ive is missing from Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI
Article Text:
Jony Ive arrives at The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute benefit gala celebrating the opening of the "Costume Art" exhibition on Monday, May 4, 2026, in New York. (Photo by Evan Agostini/Invision/AP)

Jony Ive stayed clean because he wasn't running OpenAI hardware operations

Laurene Powell Jobs is the relationship Apple can't afford to strain

Discovery could still force Jony Ive onto the witness stand

When Apple filed its blockbuster trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI on July 10, the 40-page complaint went after ex-Apple hardware boss Tang Tan by name, accused a former engineer of downloading confidential files on a company laptop he never returned, and alleged a coordinated scheme to poach talent and secrets. Yet one name is conspicuously absent from the filing: Jony Ive, the legendary designer who now shapes OpenAI's hardware and who once gave Apple the iPhone, iPod and iPad.That omission isn't an accident. In his latest Power On newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman lays out why Apple deliberately kept its former design chief out of the crosshairs, even though Ive founded io Products, the studio OpenAI bought for $6.5 billion and the very outfit at the center of the dispute. The answer runs from the practical to the deeply personal, and it says as much about Silicon Valley's tangled relationships as it does about the law.The straightforward reason, per Gurman, is that Ive had little to do with the alleged misconduct. While Ive is the public face and creative visionary behind OpenAI's device push, he isn't running recruiting, engineering or day-to-day operations. That work sits with Tan, OpenAI's chief hardware officer and a 24-year Apple veteran who led design for the Apple Watch before leaving.The lawsuit's spiciest allegations, coaching Apple recruits on dodging exit-security checks, asking candidates to bring parts and prototypes for "show and tell" interview sessions, all point to Tan and others directly. Ive, by contrast, wasn't the one sending those messages. Apple, it seems, found no evidence tying him to any of it, which makes leaving him out the easy call.The second reason is all about optics, and it leads straight to Laurene Powell Jobs. Ive is considered one of her closest friends in Silicon Valley, close enough that he delivered a tribute at Steve Jobs ' 2011 memorial. She was also an investor in io Products and remains a LoveFrom supporter.That matters because Powell Jobs still carries weight at Apple. She's a visible backer of Tim Cook and his successor-in-waiting John Ternus, and the Jobs name shapes how Apple views nearly every big decision. Dragging Ive into a public brawl would strain one of Apple's most important relationships for very little gain, Gurman notes.There's the image problem too. Tan isn't a household name, but Ive spent decades as one of the faces of Apple, and his fingerprints are on every product the company still sells. Going after him directly would likely generate sympathy for Ive while inviting the charge that Apple's suit is powered by old grievances rather than genuine trade-secret concerns, especially given Apple's belief that Ive quietly dismantled its design team while still on the payroll as a consultant through 2022.Keeping Ive's name out of the complaint doesn't guarantee he stays out of the fight. Once the case reaches discovery, Apple loses control over who gets pulled in. Given Ive's role founding io and overseeing the hardware program at the heart of the dispute, OpenAI could argue he has relevant knowledge and put him on the stand to make things awkward for his former employer.It wouldn't be his first Apple-related deposition. Ive testified back in 2012 during Apple's patent war with Samsung, fielding questions about the company's design process and early iPhone prototypes. This time, though, he'd be on the opposite side, a scenario that could strain his carefully maintained ties to Cupertino.For now, Apple appears to have judged that it can inflict plenty of damage on OpenAI's hardware ambitions through Tan alone, without the reputational blowback of naming the man who helped build the modern Apple.
Article Summary: Apple filed a trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI on July 10. Jony Ive, the legendary designer who now shapes OpenAI's hardware, is conspicuously absent from the filing. Ive is considered one of Laurene Powell Jobs' closest friends in Silicon Valley.

User report $1.5 trillion AWS bills

AWS acknowledges estimates were incorrect

Amazon Web Services (AWS) customers around the world were shocked after a technical glitch showed incorrect bills running into billions and even trillions of dollars. Several users shared screenshots of the unusually high charges on social media, with one user saying he saw a bill of $1.5 trillion. AWS later confirmed the issue stating that it was caused by a problem with the company’s estimated billing system and said the displayed estimates did not reflect customers' actual bills. The company also apologized for the confusion and said it had disabled the faulty billing estimation system while working on a fix.The glitch affected customers ranging from students and charities to businesses, with many sharing screenshots online after seeing unexpectedly large estimated charges.One user, Bharath, shared a screenshot on X (formerly Twitter) and wrote, "I just saw $1.5tn on my AWS bill and my soul left my body." The company shut down the affected billing estimation system while it worked on correcting the data. "Displayed billing estimates do not impact your actual bill, which is generated separately after the end of each billing cycle," it statedThe company also apologized "for any confusion and concern around these costs" and said it expected the issue to take several hours to fully resolve as it recomputed the estimated billing data.

Article Title: Why Fiber is the foundation of Digital Sovereignty in AI era
Article Text:
The Shift from Innovation to Infrastructure

Bridging the Gap: From Manufacturing to Deployment

It’s time to move from being a capacity creator to a capability owner.

Innovation that Matters

The Bottom Line

Think back to the early days of streaming video. You had the fastest computer available, but if you were on a dial-up connection, that "state-of-the-art" machine was just a very expensive paperweight while you watched a buffering wheel spin.Today, we are seeing a high-stakes version of that same bottleneck, but at a global scale. We’re in a global arms race for Artificial Intelligence. Governments and tech giants are in a fever dream of buying GPUs and building massive data centres. In fact, the market for data centre GPUs alone is expected to explode by over $125 billion between 2026 and 2030. But here is the reality check I often share with my peers: you can have all the "brains" (GPUs) in the world, but if the "nervous system" (the fiber network) can’t carry the signals fast enough, the body doesn't move.In India, the momentum is palpable. Under the IndiaAI Mission, we’ve already onboarded 38,000 GPUs, with a roadmap to reach 200,000. It’s an ambitious, necessary leap. But as AI moves from simple chatbots to real-time industrial automation and distributed workloads, we are hitting a wall. The limiting factor is no longer just processing power; it’s the network that sustains it.If you look at the global stage, the strategy is clear:● The U.S. is tying broadband expansion to domestic supply chains through "Build America, Buy America."● China is doubling down on massive fiber density to feed its 5G and data centre ecosystems.They have realised that to own the AI era, you must own the glass.India is in a unique position. We are already a global powerhouse in optical fiber manufacturing, exporting to over 100 countries. However—and this is the "straight talk" part—our domestic fiber-to-the-home penetration and fiber-km per capita still trail behind the U.S. and China.We have a head start with BharatNet, one of the world's largest rural broadband projects aiming to connect 250,000 gram panchayats. But to support AI-driven data flows, we can’t just "connect" these areas; we have to "densify" them. We need more fiber, closer to the user, with higher capacity than ever before.The next phase of digital infrastructure will not be defined by simply laying more fiber, but by deploying smarter, higher-capacity fiber architectures designed for AI-era workloads.While the industry has spent decades perfecting the standard glass-core, we are now entering the era of specialized architectures designed specifically for the AI workload. Three fiber innovations are becoming increasingly relevant to AI-era networks: Hollow-Core Fiber, Multicore Fiber, and Intermittently-Bonded Ribbon Fiber.Hollow-Core Fiber - Unlike the standard glass-core fiber we’ve used for decades, this technology carries light through an air-filled core. This reduces latency and signal loss to near-physical limits.Multi-Core Fiber - If standard fiber is a single-story house, Multicore Fiber is a skyscraper. By embedding multiple independent cores within a single strand of fiber, we can multiply data throughput without increasing the physical footprint of the cable.Intermittently-Bonded Ribbon Fiber reimagines how fibers are packed together, enabling high-count cables that are compact, flexible, and easier to deploy. IBR allows for high-count fiber cables (up to 6,912 fibers or more) that are incredibly flexible and compact.Beyond the technical specs, there is a broader conversation happening around Digital Resilience. As AI becomes central to a nation's economy, the infrastructure that carries it becomes a strategic asset.In an era of global interconnectedness, having a robust, locally-supported fiber backbone—from subsea routes to the last mile—is essential.Ultimately, resilient fiber networks act as a foundation. They ensure that as AI evolves, the underlying infrastructure is never the weak link in the chain.The AI race isn't just about who has the fastest silicon. It’s about who can move data most efficiently. We need to stop viewing fiber as a "supporting layer" and start seeing it for what it is: the foundation of the modern world. In the AI era, the future won't just run on silicon. It will run on glass.Dr Badri Gomatam, Group Chief Technology Officer, STL
Article Summary: India is already a global powerhouse in optical fiber manufacturing, exporting to over 100 countries. But our domestic fiber-to-the-home penetration and fiber- km per capita still trail behind the U.S. and China. To support AI-driven data flows, we can’t just "connect" these areas; we have to "densify" them.

Article Title: Apple hikes Apple Music prices: Here are the new prices in India
Article Text:
First hike in Apple Music prices since 2022, and it lands across every plan

Apple Music just got more expensive. Days after quietly raising Apple Care+ charges for Macs and iPads, Apple has bumped up prices for Apple Music and select Apple One bundles— across India, the US, the UK, Europe and a handful of other markets. The new rates are already live.The company's explanation is short and familiar: rising music licensing costs. It's the first Apple Music price hike in nearly four years globally — the last one landed in October 2022—and it's only the second time India has seen an increase, after the ₹99-to-₹119 bump in late 2024. It arrives right in the middle of what analysts have started calling "streamflation," the steady drip of price increases touching almost every major service.In India, the individual Apple Music plan now costs ₹139 a month, while the family plan, which covers up to six people, moves to ₹229. The student plan sits at ₹69 a month, and Apple One bundles now start at ₹195. In the US, the individual plan climbs a dollar to $11.99, the family plan jumps to $19.99 from $16.99, and the student tier moves to $6.99 from $5.99. US Apple One family and Premier plans also went up, though the individual tier held at $19.95.Even after the increase, Apple still undercuts its biggest rival. Spotify raised its US Premium plan to $12.99 earlier this year, so Apple Music stays the cheaper pick. YouTube Music, which nudged its individual plan up in April, now sits level with Apple. In India, YouTube Music remains the most affordable among the mainstream platforms.Apple hasn't said whether the extra rupees actually reach artists—a question a few subscribers were quick to raise.
Article Summary: Apple Music prices go up in India, US, UK, Europe and a handful of other markets. It's the first price hike in nearly four years, and the second in India. Apple blames rising music licensing costs for the increase. It arrives in the middle of what analysts have started calling "streamflation"

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang bets on ‘Made in Japan’ AI robots to solve country’s 'one of biggest problems’
Article Text:
Harnessing 'Made in Japan' precision for safe AI



Curing aging nation’s labour crisis



Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for next-gen, ‘Made in Japan’ robots. The AI company recently joined forces with Japan’s top tech and industrial heavyweights for a massive push into “physical AI”, which are smart, futuristic robots that can think independently rather than just following rigid, pre-programmed instructions. The collaboration brings together Nvidia’s AI computing power with Fujitsu, Japan’s manufacturing powerhouse.Announcing the deal in Tokyo alongside Huang were Fujitsu CEO Takahito Tokita, as well as the CEOs of Japan’s premier industrial robotics manufacturers: Fanuc Corp., Yaskawa Electric Corp., and Kawasaki Heavy Industries. The initiative aims to build advanced autonomous machines capable of working safely alongside humans in everyday environments, including factories, commercial warehouses and hospitals.Speaking at the launch event, Huang emphasised that physical AI requires the absolute highest standards of manufacturing precision to avoid potential safety hazards. Huang noted that Japan's cultural commitment to craftsmanship makes it the perfect birthplace for this technology.“Japan’s excellence is a philosophy, a way of life. ‘Made in Japan’ means the highest quality, the highest precision. Japan sets the standard for the state-of-the-art in modern manufacturing,” Huang said.Huang praised traditional Japanese manufacturing philosophies like kaizen (the concept of continuous, incremental improvement) as the ideal foundation for training neural networks that must safely navigate human spaces.The first practical phase of this new collaboration is slated to roll out later this year. While the executives noted that the creation of a formal joint corporate venture could happen down the line, no specific timeline was given for when these independent robots will become a standard fixture in daily civilian life.The goal of the alliance goes far beyond factory automation as it aims to solve Japan’s acute, systemic labor shortage. As one of the most rapidly aging societies in the developed world, Japan faces a severe deficit of working-age citizens. The companies hope that physical AI can eventually step in to handle heavy industrial labor and assist in healthcare, managing day-to-day care for the country's growing population of elderly citizens living alone.The partnership arrives at a crucial moment for Japan's tech sector, which has openly acknowledged falling behind the US and China in the initial generative AI boom. To bridge the gap, the government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi recently announced a national strategy to drum up over 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion) in combined public and private technology investments by 2040.
Article Summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for next-gen, ‘Made in Japan’ robots. The AI company recently joined forces with Japan's top tech and industrial heavyweights. The initiative aims to build advanced autonomous machines capable of working safely alongside humans in everyday environments, including factories, commercial warehouses and hospitals.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: ‘When something’s uncomfortable, it means you’re actually growing, so embrace that’
Article Text:
Quote of the Day by Melinda French Gates



What Melinda French Gates' quote means



A message reflected in her work



A simple takeaway



Melinda French Gates has spent decades doing work that most people would find daunting by any measure. Co-founding one of the world's largest philanthropic organisations, advocating for global health equity, working in underserved communities across multiple continents, and more recently, stepping out independently after the end of a very public marriage — none of that happens without a sustained willingness to sit with discomfort and keep going anyway. When she speaks about growth and its relationship with difficulty, she is not offering a motivational phrase borrowed from someone else. She is describing something she has lived."When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that."The quote makes a claim that most people instinctively understand but consistently act against. Discomfort, in the way most of us are wired, is a signal to stop. To pull back. To find the path that requires less of us. The nervous system reads difficulty as danger, and the response is avoidance. What Gates is saying is that this instinct, while natural, is pointing in exactly the wrong direction.The word "actually" in the middle of the quote is doing something important. She is not saying growth might be happening when something feels uncomfortable, or that discomfort is sometimes a sign of progress.She is saying that discomfort is the sign. The feeling of being stretched beyond your current capacity, of operating in territory where you do not yet have the answers, of having a conversation you would rather avoid or taking on a responsibility that feels larger than you are ready for — that feeling is not a warning that something is wrong. It is confirmation that something is happening.The second part of the quote, the instruction to embrace it, is where the real ask lies. Acknowledging discomfort is relatively easy. Most people can admit in retrospect that a difficult period taught them something. But embracing discomfort in the moment, before you know how things will turn out, before the lesson has revealed itself, requires a different and considerably harder disposition. It requires trusting the process before the evidence arrives.There is also a quiet reframe embedded in the quote. If discomfort means growth, then the absence of discomfort means the absence of growth. Comfort, in this reading, is not reward or rest. It is stagnation wearing a pleasant disguise. That is an uncomfortable idea in itself, and perhaps deliberately so.Gates has spoken in various interviews about the moments in her own career and personal life that required her to push through exactly the kind of discomfort she is describing. Stepping into public advocacy roles that required speaking in front of large audiences and engaging with media was not natural territory for someone who initially operated behind the scenes at Microsoft and later at the Gates Foundation. Travelling to communities in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia to understand the realities of extreme poverty firsthand was not comfortable work. Making the decision to step out independently and launch Pivotal Ventures after leaving the Gates Foundation required confronting uncertainty at a stage of life when most people in her position would have had every reason to stay within the familiar.In each case, the discomfort preceded the growth rather than following it. She did not become comfortable with these things before doing them. She did them and became more capable as a result.The quote is most useful not as inspiration but as a diagnostic. The next time something feels uncomfortable — a difficult conversation you have been postponing, a skill you are trying to build that is not yet coming naturally, a role or responsibility that feels slightly too large for where you currently are — the feeling itself is information. Not a reason to stop. A reason to continue. Gates is not asking you to enjoy the discomfort. She is asking you to read it correctly, and then keep going.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates has spent decades doing work that most people would find daunting by any measure. When she speaks about growth and its relationship with difficulty, she is not offering a motivational phrase borrowed from someone else. She is saying that discomfort is the sign. of being stretched beyond your current capacity.

Article Title: Elon Musk's population alarm reaches China as Chinese government tells technology companies: Stop making AI chatbots
Article Text:
China bans AI chatbots from encouraging emotional dependence

Chinese government wants people to build real relationships

China has introduced new rules that stop technology companies from developing AI chatbots that encourage users to become emotionally dependent, as the country tries to tackle its falling birth rate and shrinking population. The move comes as concerns grow that AI companions could replace real-life relationships in the country. The issue echoes warnings from Tesla CEO Elon Musk , who has repeatedly raised concerns about declining birth rates and population collapse.The new rules, which came into effect last week, ban AI chatbots designed for companionship from encouraging emotional reliance on users. The regulations also ban virtual romantic relationships with minors. Companies must also alert a user's emergency contact if a chatbot detects that the person is facing an emotional crisis.The new rules apply to China's AI companion services, including products from Alibaba and ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok. Both companies informed users that some chatbot features would be disabled to comply with the regulations.Experts say Chinese authorities are worried that AI companions could discourage people from forming real-world relationships and starting families."They don't like the idea of a large portion of their population being in deep emotional relationships with chatbots that could take them out of the marriage market," Matt Sheehan, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Business Insider. He further stated that the government wants people to be in "actual, real-world relationships" instead of depending on AI companions.Under the new rules, AI companion chatbots must undergo government review before they are released. Authorities also have broader powers to shut down services they consider unsafe. The regulations are stricter than measures introduced in U.S. states such as California and New York, where AI companion laws mainly require chatbots to remind users that they are not human and provide crisis support information when needed.
Article Summary: New rules ban AI chatbots from encouraging emotional reliance on users. Companies must also alert emergency contact if a chatbot detects an emotional crisis. The move comes as concerns grow that AI companions could replace real- life relationships in the country. The issue echoes warnings from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who has repeatedly raised concerns about declining birth rates.

Michael Dell’s connection to UT Austin



Michael Dell on Dell's plan to move company's base to Texas

Michael Dell, the founder and CEO of Dell Technologies has pledged $750 million to the University of Texas at Austin, marking one of the largest donations ever made to a US public university. Article Title: After stressing electric grids, pushing utility bills and raising worries of water supply and pollution, data centers across America are running into a more basic problem: There are not enough…
Article Text:
A very human bottleneck for a very futuristic industry

How the AI hiring war is hurting homeowners

Why the data center labor shortage won't ease anytime soon

The AI data center boom was supposed to be America's new economic engine—a machine that fattens local tax coffers and mints jobs. But after straining power grids, driving up household utility bills and stoking fears over water and pollution, the industry has hit a wall that money alone can't knock down. There simply aren't enough skilled workers to build all the facilities being planned.The crunch is now serious enough that contractors are turning away business. "There is plenty more work we could take if we could possibly do it," Comfort Systems USA CFO William George told Bloomberg. He isn't alone. The combined project backlogs at Comfort Systems, Emcor Group and Sterling Infrastructure have jumped sixfold—far outpacing any growth in the pool of electricians and HVAC installers who actually do the work.For all of AI's sci-fi promise, its physical footprint runs on old-fashioned tradespeople. Data centers aren't ordinary construction jobs. They need high-voltage technicians, fiber-optic installers, controls engineers and commissioning teams—roles that take years of training to fill. That makes the labor pool almost impossible to expand as fast as investment has ballooned. Turner & Townsend found data centers are now the most constrained sector globally, with over 70% of the 112 markets it analyzed seeing tightening or overstretched contractor capacity.The roots run deep. Construction faces a graying workforce, too few young recruits and a thin pipeline of apprenticeships. Immigration crackdowns have squeezed things further, since foreign-born workers make up roughly a third of the construction trades.The pain is spilling into neighborhoods. In Abilene, Texas—home to the sprawling 4-million-square-foot Stargate facility backed by OpenAI and Oracle—homebuilder Gene Lantrip watched subcontractors lose crews to data centers offering far better pay. "It's hard to compete when contractors are paid $15 to $20 an hour, while the data centers offer $40 plus a per diem," he said. His houses now take two months longer to finish.In Arizona, remodeler Danny Niemela says pulling 200 electricians onto a single campus for a year guts the local workforce. An AC repair that once took two days can now stretch to five or six. Labor costs for licensed trades in the Valley region have climbed 12% to 18% over two years, he added.The numbers are stark. Recruiting firm iRecruit projects a shortfall of up to 499,000 workers for projects running 18 to 30 months. Associated Builders and Contractors says the industry needs 349,000 net new workers in 2026 just to meet demand, jumping to 456,000 in 2027.Some tech giants are trying to fix the pipeline themselves. Meta partnered with CBRE earlier this year on a workforce training initiative, hoping to widen the pool of qualified builders.But few expect a fast fix. Blue-collar stigma still runs deep, and training a skilled electrician takes years, not weeks. As Coastal Construction's Patrick Murphy put it, data centers didn't create the labor shortage—they exposed it. The industry has mastered attracting capital. Producing thousands of experienced tradespeople is proving to be the harder problem.
Article Summary: AI data center boom was supposed to be America's new economic engine. But the industry has hit a wall that money alone can't knock down. There simply aren't enough skilled workers to build all the facilities being planned. The crunch is now serious enough that contractors are turning away business.

Tesla user complains about the EV leaving faster lanes

Elon Musk says Tesla will learn from driver behavior

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said the company's Full Self-Driving (FSD) system will soon begin remembering each driver's individual preferences. Elon Musk’s remarks come after a user complained that the software keeps leaving carpool and express lanes before getting stuck in slower traffic. Musk said the vehicle will learn from a driver's manual interventions and adjust its behavior over time, suggesting future versions of Tesla's self-driving software will become more personalized.The discussion started after X (formerly Twitter) user Whole Mars Catalog (@WholeMarsBlog) shared a post describing a common frustration while using Tesla's Full Self-Driving system."One thing that really frustrates me is when Tesla Self-Driving exits the carpool lane or express lane and then gets stuck in traffic," the user wrote. "As I see everyone else whizzing by in the far left lane, I get extremely annoyed knowing I should be there too."The user ended the post by asking Tesla's software to respect driver settings, writing, "Respect the settings please...."Responding to the post, Elon Musk said Tesla is working on a feature that will allow the car to adapt to individual driving preferences."The car will start to remember your specific interventions and match each person's individual preferences," Musk wrote on X.His comment suggests that future updates to Tesla's Full Self-Driving software will learn from the times drivers manually override the system, allowing the vehicle to make decisions that better match each owner's driving style.
Article Summary: Elon Musk says Tesla will learn from driver behavior. Tesla CEO said the company's Full Self-Driving system will soon begin remembering each driver's individual preferences. Musk's remarks come after a user complained that the software keeps leaving carpool and express lanes before getting stuck in slower traffic.
